A "byte" is eight bits. Hexadecimal values are written 0x2A. All multi-byte integers are unsigned and are sent in network byte order (big-endian, most significant byte first).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: ETP is a small file-transfer protocol. A client opens a connection to a server, identifies itself, asks for one thing - a directory listing, a file, or permission to store a file - and leaves. The server keeps a single flat directory of files, its root, and serves any number of clients at once.
texts.text: ETP is a small file-transfer protocol. A client opens a connection to a server, identifies itself, asks for one thing - a directory listing, a file, or permission to store a file - and leaves. The server keeps a single flat directory of files, its root, and serves any number of clients at once.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: ETP is an application-layer protocol. It assumes the layer below it delivers a reliable, ordered byte stream and nothing more. In PA1 that layer is TCP. In the final project it is the transport you build over UDP in PA2. Your application code reaches the network only through a small transport seam (Section 11), so that the swap touches only the transport files and the Makefile.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: TCP delivers a byte stream, not messages. The 8-byte header you send with one call may arrive in two pieces, or glued to the end of the previous message, or together with the next three. A receiver MUST read the header with a loop that keeps reading until it has exactly 8 bytes (the recv_exact of Chapter 5, §5.8), then read exactly LENGTH more the same way. A single recv(8) works on your laptop most of the time and fails in grading.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 1. The first request on a session MUST be HELLO. Any other request type (0x02-0x05) arriving in AWAIT_HELLO is answered with ERROR NOT_READY and the server closes the connection. Header errors and other types are handled first, exactly as in Section 8.1: a TYPE outside 0x01-0x05, or a HELLO with a bad name, gets a non-fatal ERROR and the session stays in AWAIT_HELLO.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 2. In READY, the client may send any number of LIST, GET and PUT requests, then BYE.
texts.text: In READY, the client may send any number of LIST, GET and PUT requests, then BYE.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 3. Ordering. A server MUST process the requests on one connection in the order they arrive and send exactly one response to each request it processes, in the same order. After a fatal error it processes nothing further. The clients in this course send one request and wait for its response, but a server MUST NOT assume that: several complete requests may arrive in a single read.
texts.text: Ordering. A server MUST process the requests on one connection in the order they arrive and send exactly one response to each request it processes, in the same order. After a fatal error it processes nothing further. The clients in this course send one request and wait for its response, but a server MUST NOT assume that: several complete requests may arrive in a single read.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 4. Closing. After sending BYE_OK the server closes the connection. The client waits until it sees the server's close (a read returns end-of-stream) and then closes its own side. The server is therefore the side that performs the active close and holds the TIME-WAIT state: for about a minute after closing, Linux keeps the old connection's address and port pair reserved so that delayed segments from it cannot be mistaken for a new connection (Chapter 5, §5.5.3).

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: 5. If the client's connection ends without BYE - cleanly between messages, or abruptly in the middle of one - the server abandons any partial request, sends nothing, releases the connection, and carries on serving everyone else.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: LIST_OK payload: one line per file in the root, each line the file name, one TAB byte (0x09), the file size in bytes as a decimal number with no leading zeros (0 for an empty file), and one LF byte (0x0A). The lines MUST be sorted by name in ascending byte order - so Zulu.txt sorts before alpha.txt, because Z is 0x5A and a is 0x61. The listing includes only entries that are regular files and whose names are valid ETP names (Section 7); directories, symbolic links and anything else are left out. An empty root gives an empty payload. If the root cannot be read, or the listing would exceed MAX_LEN, the reply is SERVER_ERROR. A file larger than MAX_LEN is listed, but cannot be fetched (GET answers SERVER_ERROR).

The lines MUST be sorted by name in ascending byte order - so Zulu.txt sorts before alpha.txt, because Z is 0x5A and a is 0x61. The listing includes only entries that are regular files and whose names are valid ETP names (Section 7); directories, symbolic links and anything else are left out. An empty root gives an empty payload. If the root cannot be read, or the listing would exceed MAX_LEN, the reply is SERVER_ERROR. A file larger than MAX_LEN is listed, but cannot be fetched (GET answers SERVER_ERROR).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Payload: the name of the file, with no terminator. The server checks, in this order: an invalid name gives ERROR BAD_NAME; a name that is not a regular file in the root gives NOT_FOUND; a file too large for one message, or one that cannot be read, gives SERVER_ERROR. Otherwise the server replies GET_OK whose payload is the file's entire contents. All three errors are non-fatal.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The server checks, in this order: if LENGTH < 2, or NAMELEN > LENGTH - 2, the reply is BAD_REQUEST; an invalid name gives BAD_NAME; a failure to store gives SERVER_ERROR. All three are non-fatal. Otherwise the server stores DATA under that name in its root, replacing any existing file of that name, and replies PUT_OK whose 32-byte payload is the SHA-256 digest of DATA. An empty DATA is legal and stores an empty file.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If the name exists but is not a regular file (a directory, say), the reply is SERVER_ERROR; if it is a symbolic link, the link itself is replaced, never its target.
texts.text: If the name exists but is not a regular file (a directory, say), the reply is SERVER_ERROR; if it is a symbolic link, the link itself is replaced, never its target.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The server SHOULD write to a temporary file in the root and rename it into place, so a concurrent GET never sees half a file. The temporary name MUST NOT be a valid ETP name (start it with a period), so it is never listed or fetched, and it is removed if the store fails. If two clients PUT the same name at once, the last rename wins.

texts.orig: The client MUST compute the SHA-256 of the data it sent and compare it with the digest it receives. A mismatch means the file did not arrive intact (Section 10). The digest covers DATA exactly as received; the server need not read the file back.

texts.orig: The pattern must match the whole name. In Python, use re.fullmatch, or end the pattern with \Z: a plain $ also matches just before a final newline, so re.match would accept alpha.txt followed by a newline. In C, check every byte against the rule; never treat a name as a C string, because alpha.txt followed by a zero byte and more text is not a valid name.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: For a fatal error the server sends the ERROR response and then closes the connection; it need not process anything further. Closing a socket that still has unread bytes waiting makes TCP send a reset, which on some systems can discard the ERROR before the client reads it. So the transport's close SHOULD shut down its sending side (shutdown(SHUT_WR)), read and discard whatever is still arriving until end-of-stream or about a second passes, and only then close. That logic belongs inside close in your transport file, not in your server. A client MAY therefore see a reset instead of the ERROR after a fatal error, and treats it as exit status 2. For a non-fatal error the server sends the ERROR response and the session continues in the same state: the request's whole payload has been consumed, so the next byte is the start of the next request.

texts.orig: · --port and --root are required. --bind defaults to 127.0.0.1: the server listens on loopback unless told otherwise, which keeps it inside the course's authorised scope.

texts.orig: · If an argument is missing or invalid (a non-numeric port, a port outside 1-65535, a DIR that is not a directory, an unknown option), or the port cannot be bound, the server prints a message on standard error and exits with a non-zero status.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · The server runs until it is killed (SIGINT or SIGTERM). No clean-up is required.
texts.text: The server runs until it is killed (SIGINT or SIGTERM). No clean-up is required.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Concurrency. The server MUST serve at least 16 simultaneous sessions, and a session whose client has stalled part-way through a message MUST NOT delay any other session. One thread per connection is the expected design; an event loop is also fine. Serving one connection at a time is not.
texts.text: Concurrency. The server MUST serve at least 16 simultaneous sessions, and a session whose client has stalled part-way through a message MUST NOT delay any other session. One thread per connection is the expected design; an event loop is also fine. Serving one connection at a time is not.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Robustness. A client that vanishes at any moment - including while the server is in the middle of sending it 2 MiB - affects only its own session. The server process MUST NOT exit, and it MUST release the connection.
texts.text: Robustness. A client that vanishes at any moment - including while the server is in the middle of sending it 2 MiB - affects only its own session. The server process MUST NOT exit, and it MUST release the connection.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Restart. The server MUST be able to restart on the same port immediately, while old connections are still in TIME-WAIT.
texts.text: Restart. The server MUST be able to restart on the same port immediately, while old connections are still in TIME-WAIT.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Files. The server serves only regular files directly inside its root. A symbolic link is never a regular file for ETP purposes: it is not listed, and GET answers NOT_FOUND.
texts.text: Files. The server serves only regular files directly inside its root. A symbolic link is never a regular file for ETP purposes: it is not listed, and GET answers NOT_FOUND.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Idle sessions. A server MAY close, without sending anything, a session from which no byte has arrived for 60 seconds.
texts.text: Idle sessions. A server MAY close, without sending anything, a session from which no byte has arrived for 60 seconds.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: · Logging. The server MUST write one line to standard output for every response it sends (including ERRORs), and flush it. Standard output carries nothing but these lines; any other message goes to standard error. Lines from different sessions MUST NOT interleave. The fields, separated by single spaces, are: the local time when the response is sent, as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.mmm; the client's address and port as address:port; the request's type name (HELLO, . . . , BYE), or 0x and two hex digits for any TYPE outside 0x01-0x05; the status code sent (0 for success); and the LENGTH from the request's header, even if the payload was never read:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The server dies when a client disconnects. In C, writing to a connection the peer has reset raises SIGPIPE, which kills the process by default. Pass MSG_NOSIGNAL to send() or ignore the signal with signal(SIGPIPE, SIG_IGN), then handle the EPIPE error. Python raises BrokenPipeError or ConnectionResetError instead; catch them per connection.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One slow client freezes everyone. If your accept loop handles a connection before accepting the next, a client that sends half a header holds the whole server hostage. That is a denial-of-service in miniature (Chapter 5, §5.9).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: All three options are required and come before the command, in any order. The client does not check NAME or REMOTE against the ETP rules: it sends them as given and the server's answer decides.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Each run is one session: connect; send HELLO with NAME; perform the one command; send BYE; wait for BYE_OK and then for the server to close; close; exit. A reset instead of a clean close after BYE_OK still counts as success. A client MAY give up on a silent server after a timeout of its choosing.

texts.orig: Checking a response. For each response header the client checks, in order: VERSION is 1; LENGTH is at most MAX_LEN; TYPE is the expected . . . _OK or ERROR. Only then does it read the payload. A PUT_OK whose LENGTH is not 32 is a protocol failure.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Your server and client MUST reach the network only through a transport module that offers the six operations below, and nothing else in your code may use the operating system's socket interface. That means: in Python, the socket module; in C, the headers sys/socket.h, netinet/in.h and netdb.h, and the C library's own socket(), bind(), listen(), accept(), connect(), send(), recv() (and their to/from forms), setsockopt(), shutdown() and getaddrinfo(). Your seam's own functions are not the operating system's, even when they share a name: calling transport.listen() or tp_accept() from your server is exactly the point. Byte-order conversion is not networking: arpa/inet.h for htonl and ntohl, and Python's struct, may be used anywhere. Your own test programs, kept in a tests/ folder or named test_*, are exempt. In PA1 the module wraps TCP. In the final project you will write a second module with the same six operations over your PA2 transport, and switch to it without touching your ETP code. If the seam is clean, that switch is an afternoon. If socket calls are scattered through your server, it is a rewrite.

texts.orig: The C starter declares the operations in transport.h and defines them in transport_tcp.c. In the Python starter they are written in transport_tcp.py, and your programs import them through transport.py, whose one line chooses the transport: in the project you change that line and nothing else. You may change the signatures to suit your design, but keep the six operations, keep them in files whose names begin with transport, and keep every socket call inside those files.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One session, every byte. The client is named eagle01; the root holds Zulu.txt (5 bytes) and alpha.txt, whose 12 bytes are Hello, ETP! and a newline. The client lists the root, fetches alpha.txt, stores Go Eagles! plus a newline as notes.txt, asks for a file that does not exist, and says goodbye. The server's name and the error text are free-form; yours will differ, and so will those messages' lengths. In each message the first 8 bytes are the header. This table was produced by the reference encoder, not typed.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Everything is in the clear. Anyone who can see the traffic reads every file name, every file, and every client name, and could alter them in flight. The SHA-256 digest in PUT_OK detects accidental corruption; it does not stop an attacker who can rewrite both the data and the digest. Confidentiality and integrity against an attacker is one of the project extensions.

Writes the GET_OK payload to the local file LOCAL, replacing it if it exists. On any failure, LOCAL is not created or changed.

table_cells.text: The server answered with ERROR. Print the code and the text on standard error. If the code is a non-fatal one from Table 2 and the failed request was not HELLO, the session is still open in READY: the client SHOULD still send BYE and close normally. Otherwise it just closes.
Anything else went wrong: bad arguments, cannot connect, the connection ended early, a response that fails the checks above, a local file that cannot be read or written.
put only: the PUT_OK digest does not match the SHA-256 of the data sent. (The client still sends BYE; the exit status stays 3.)

table_cells.text: Start accepting sessions on addr:port. Returns a listener.
Wait for the next session. Returns a connection and the peer's address and port, for logging.
Open a session to a server. Returns a connection. Hand every byte to the transport, in order, or report
failure. Never a partial send. Return exactly n bytes. If the stream ends before any of them arrives, report a clean close (the peer finished between messages); if it ends part-way, report an
error. Finish the session gracefully: shut down the sending side, read and discard until end-of-stream or about a second passes, then close (Section 8). A seventh
helper to close the listener is fine.
